description: Born from a shared drive to master avionics and autonomous systems, Team Lunar Rangers 007 is bringing terrestrial engineering logic to the lunar surface. It's Interesting to that there could be more resources in south pole but the solar system itself overwhelming the travel there is saddening. But hey, we won't settle for less, right. So We are building a visual navigation and resource mapping tool to simulate and navigate to the Moon's South pole.
summary: HORIZON OPS is an interactive 3D lunar mission control and planning web application for the Moon's South Pole. It lets anyone click on real NASA elevation maps of the lunar south pole to check whether a spacecraft can land safely, see exactly when sunlight (solar power) and Earth communication signals will reach that spot, compare what breaks if a launch is delayed by 48 hours, and plan a safe rover driving route from a sunlit Base Pod into dark craters that hold water ice.
details:
HORIZON OPS (LR-007) — Lunar South Pole Landing Site, Mission Window, LunaDiff & Rover Traverse Navigator

Github repo: Horizon Ops

1. What Does It Do & How Does It Work?

HORIZON OPS is an interactive 3D and 2D lunar mission control and surface planning web application built for the Lunar South Pole (80°S–90°S). It enables mission planners, researchers, and students to evaluate spacecraft touchdown safety, solar power availability, Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication links, launch-delay trade- offs, and energy-constrained rover traverses into water-ice Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs) using authentic NASA planetary datasets.

How It Works:

1. Dual-View 3D Globe & 2D Polar Map (80°S–90°S): Combines a CesiumJS 3D lunar globe textured with NASA LROC Wide Angle Camera (luna_wac_global) imagery, high-resolution 129 × 129 (20 m spacing) NASA LOLA DEM 3D terrain patches across four Artemis-era candidate sites (Connecting Ridge [Site 01], Shackleton Rim [Site 04], Malapert Mountain [Site 07], and Haworth Interior [Site 09]), and an interactive 2D Polar Map supporting arbitrary coordinate clicks.

2. Touchdown Slope Safety & Nearby Safe Haven Recommender: Evaluates local terrain steepness against Artemis / CLPS lander limits (SAFE < 8.0°, CAUTION 8.0°–15.0°, HAZARD > 15.0°) with live 3D shader switching. If a selected location is hazardous or shadow-trapped, the Safe Haven Recommender scans surrounding concentric rings (5–20 km) to recommend nearby flat ridges (e.g., Connecting Ridge Site 01 Safe Havens at 0.44°, 2.61°, and 1.36°).

3. Curvature-Aware 360° Horizon Ray-Casting & Solar Disc Penumbra: Traces 1,440 horizon rays (0.25° azimuth spacing out to 150 km) accounting for exact lunar spherical curvature drop (Δz = √(R² + d²) - R with R = 1, 737, 400 m), and evaluates 14-day (30-minute cadence) topocentric Sun and Earth trajectories from NASA JPL Horizons (DE421, MOON_ME_DE421) using partial solar disc penumbra integration rather than binary point-source approximations.

4. LunaDiff Engine ("See What Changed. See Why."): Compares a Nominal Launch Window (Nov 15, 2026) against a +48h Launch Delay side by side (e.g., quantifying a -46.2 h sunlight loss and +10.0 h Earth DTE shift at Site 01) and links every gained or lost interval directly to the obstructing crater rim azimuth and elevation on the 360° Horizon Inspector.

5. Dual-Mode Energy & LOS-Constrained Rover Traverse Planner: Plans surface sorties from a landed Base Pod (5 m comms mast) toward water-ice PSR craters (Shackleton Floor, Shoemaker, Cabeus [LCROSS], Faustini, de Gerlache) in both Manual Mode (adaptive 0.45×–1.32× radial steps + target snap) and Automatic Mode (multi-waypoint solver), enforcing ≤ 15° slope limits, a 1,200 Wh battery with 20% safety floor, 150W drive draw, 350 W solar array charging, SOLAR_REGEN_HOLD recharge stops, and curvature-corrected Base Pod-to-rover (2 m mast) radio line-of-sight.

2. What Benefits Does It Have?

• Causal Root-Cause Diagnostics: Instead of only reporting average illumination percentages, LunaDiff explains when a blackout happens and which exact mountain ridge azimuth causes it when a launch slips by 24–72 hours.

• End-to-End Surface Operations in One Cockpit: Unifies landing site selection, solar/comms window analysis, and post-touchdown PSR rover pathfinding in a single browser workspace.

• 100% Offline & Browser-Standalone Resilience: Bundled NASA LOLA binary meshes (. bin), precomputed 360° horizons, SHA-256 cached JPL Horizons fixtures, and an in- browser physics fallback engine allow the entire application to run instantaneously on static cloud hosting or completely offline without requiring expensive cloud GPUs.

• Auditable Scientific Integrity: Missing DEM pixels fail closed (NaN -> UNKNOWN) rather than fabricating flat terrain, and one-click JSON / CSV exports embed MOON_ME_DE421 coordinates and SHA-256 dataset provenance.

3. What Is the Intended Impact of the Project?

• Accelerating Artemis-Era South Pole Mission Design: Gives mission designers and robotic traverse planners a fast, visually transparent tool to evaluate how launch schedule slips and local ridge relief affect lander survival and water-ice prospecting sorties.

• Democratizing Planetary Engineering Worldwide (Built in Sri Lanka for the World): By combining open NASA LOLA and JPL Horizons data with an offline-capable web architecture hosted on Google Firebase, universities, student teams, and STEM educators anywhere in the world can run authentic Lunar South Pole mission simulations directly in a standard web browser at zero cost.

4. What Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software Did You Use?

• Coding Languages: Python 3.14, TypeScript 5.9, JavaScript (ES2022), HTML5, CSS3.

• Frontend & 3D Visualization: React 19.2, Vite 7.2, Tailwind CSS 4.1, CesiumJS (cesium ^1.147), Three.js (^0.181) & @react-three/fiber (^9.4), Recharts (^3.0), Lucide React (^0.468), Google Fonts (Inter, JetBrains Mono).

• Backend & Scientific Computing: FastAPI (>=0.162.7), Pydantic v2 (>=2.12), Uvicorn (>=0.54), NumPy (>=2.1), SciPy (>=1.10), PyProj (>=3.5), Rasterio (>=1.5.2), Tifffile (>=2026.11), ImageCodecs (>=2026.11).

• Testing, Contracts & Cloud Hosting: JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 (jsonschema 4.25.1), Pytest (153 backend + 8 contract tests), Node.js Test Runner (23 frontend tests — 184 automated passing tests total), Git & GitHub Actions CI, and Google Firebase Hosting (web.app) via the 2026 NASA Space Apps Global Collaborator (Google) offer.

• Hardware: Standard personal laptops (CPU-only memory-mapped GeoTIFF processing and WebGL browser rendering—no dedicated GPU cluster required).

• SI Development Assistants: ChatGPT, OpenAI Codex, and Google Antigravity were used for UI/API scaffolding, test scripting, and documentation formatting; all runtime lunar physics and pathfinding are 100% deterministic.

5. How Is Your Project Creative?

• "Git-Diff" for Space Mission Windows (LunaDiff): Treating launch delays like a visual diff—where mission planners can click any red "lost sunlight/comms" bar on a timeline and immediately see the offending crater wall highlighted on a 360° horizon skyplot—turns opaque ephemeris tables into instant geometric intuition.

• Solar-Regeneration Waypoint Holds (SOLAR_REGEN_HOLD): Rather than treating rover routing as shortest-path geometry, our traverse planner models dynamic synodic solar rotation (+0.508°/h) and schedules autonomous sunlit recharge holds (2.06 h + 0.15 h to 90% state-of-charge) on illuminated ridge crests before diving into 0% sunlit water-ice craters.

• Hybrid API + Browser Physics Architecture: Mirroring the terrain, horizon, and traverse algorithms across both the FastAPI Python engine and the TypeScript client allows full interactive 3D mission planning even on static web hosting.

6. What Factors Did Your Team Consider?

• Grazing Polar Illumination (0°–1.5°) & Distant Horizon Blockers: At 88°S–90°S, craters up to 150 km away can block the Sun, requiring multi-tier step ray-casting with exact lunar curvature drop (Δz ≈ 115.1 m at 20 km).

• Earth's 27.3-Day Libration Cycle: A sunlit ridge is unusable if Earth drops behind a northern crater rim, so DTE visibility is tracked concurrently with solar power at every 30-minute step.

• Real Spacecraft & Rover Engineering Envelopes: Touchdown slope bands (<8° / 8°–15°/ >15°), lander/pod mast heights (5 m Base Pod vs 2 m rover), battery reserve floors (≥20% of 1,200 Wh), return-to-haven energy budgets, and camera orbit floor constraints on steep 3D rims like Shackleton.

• Fail-Closed Safety & Data Provenance: Ensuring missing LOLA pixels never produce false "safe" readings, and verifying all interfaces across a 4-member engineering split using frozen JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 contracts and 184 automated tests.
